To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“Microbial carbonates are formed in a unique environment where oxic and anoxic conditions co-exist and where the microbial consortium performs anaerobic oxidation methane (AOM).”

(1) the carbonates of the Hydrate Ridge chemoherms were formed from a mixture of methane-rich fluids and seawater, (2) the carbonates are the result of the interaction of archaea and bacteria, (3) the carbonates precipitate at a depth where methane-rich fluids are in contact with seawater, and (4) the carbonates form above the seaflood as the result of a microbial consortium that performs AOM in the presence of oxygen.
1. Two active chenoherm carbonate build-ups, the Pinnacle Chemoherm and the South East Knoll Chemoherm, have been discovered and studied at Hydrate ridge on the Cascadia margin.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the formation of unique carbonate structures in an environment where the formation of carbonates is not to be expected, i.e. in a methane-rich environment.

the formation and growth of the chemo-herms, the microbial processes and the chemical reactions involved, as well as the geochemical processes and the fluid flow that are responsible for the formation and growth.
the identification and characterization of the unique microbial community that is responsible for the formation of these carbonate build-ups in the deep sea.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the formation of these unique chemoherms on the Cascadia margin is the result of the interplay between a consortium of archaea, sulfate-reducing prokaryotes and Beggiatoa, and is driven by methane oxidation in a micro-environment of low oxygen concentrations and high methane concentrations.

the chemoherm carbonate formation at Hydrate ridge is a microbially mediated process that is controlled by methane seepage from below the BSR and the presence of a consortium of anaerobic methane-oxidizing archaea and sulfate reducing bacteria.
these chemoherms are the result of the interaction between a microbial community and a fluid flow system that delivers methane to the seafloor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have discovered a unique type of chemoherm that grows into the water column and that is built from carbonates that are precipitated by a consortium of microbes that oxidize methane.
the formation of chemoherm carbonate structures is a result of the activity of a consortium of archaea (methanotrophs), sulfate-reducing (SR) bacteria and Beggiatoa.

the chemoherm carbonate build-ups are the result of a complex interaction of a consortium of archaea, sulfate-reducing, sulfur-oxidizing and nitrate-reducing bacteria and Beggiatoa in the water column and at the seafloor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the chemoherm growth is not limited to the seafloor but can extend into the water column, and that this is a unique process on the seafloor.
the chemoherm carbonate build-ups represent a novel type of microbial carbonate formation.
microbial communities can be responsible for the formation of carbonate structures that are not only restricted to shallow water environments but can also grow in the deep ocean.
